# **2\. Game Design** {#2.-game-design}

2.0 Story

The Kingdom of Velundra has known many kings. Brave kings. Fierce kings. Kings who charged headfirst into battle, sword raised, and died before their crowns had time to tarnish.

Then came King Aldric the Prudent, and everything changed.

Aldric was not born a warrior. He was born a strategist. While other kings trained their bodies, Aldric trained his mind, his tongue, and his network of loyal subjects. When the Skeleton Horde rose from the Catacombs beneath the kingdom, every advisor expected him to march. Instead, Aldric retreated to the center of his war chamber, summoned his cards, and began to think.

His enemies called it cowardice. His people called him a genius.

Now Aldric must do what he does best: survive. Not by fighting, not by fleeing. But by being the smartest person on the board.

The coward king doesn't run because he's afraid. He runs because he's already three moves ahead.

## 2.1 Summary {#2.1-summary}

### **Basic Game Description**

The Coward King is a roguelite-style game that is highly tactical. It is played on a 8x8 board, which is very similar in size to a chessboard. The game centers on a king who is both the most powerful and the weakest at the same time; this is because he cannot defend himself directly, but instead uses a hand of cards to deploy allies and political traps on the board to protect himself. The objective of the game is for the king to survive 30 turns per horde without sustaining a single scratch, and to ensure that no more than two enemies enter the king’s safe zone—which is 3x3—at the same time.

This game will have three levels, each featuring several hordes and a final boss. This adds up to a total of twelve encounters per battle. As in a good roguelite, if the king takes damage and dies, the player will return to the same level where the king died, retaining their permanent rewards purchased with the gold earned by defeating hordes and clearing levels, which are preserved after deaths.

### 

### 

### **Design Model: Roguelite** {#design-model:-roguelite}

* Permanent upgrades: the player loses gold on death but retains purchased card upgrades.

* Checkpoint system: death in Level 2 returns the player to Level 2 Horde 1, not to the very beginning. Progress is fair, so is the player .

* Randomized card hand: 3 random cards are dealt at the begging of a level, after the first horde it’s given an extra card from a pool of 15, creating variation between runs without requiring procedural level generation.

* Short sessions: each horde lasts a maximum of 30 turns (\~5-10 minutes). The full game takes 1-3 hours. This matches the roguelite principle of short, repeatable sessions.

* "One more run" loop: the combination of random hands, permanent upgrades, and visible unlockable improvements creates the compulsive loop characteristic of this genre.

**2.1.1 Story / Narrative**

The Coward King takes place in a fractured medieval kingdom where the ruler, once powerful, has become the main target of invading enemies led by rival leaders seeking to overthrow him. Unable to fight directly, the king relies on strategy, political influence, and the deployment of allies and traps to survive waves of enemies within his castle. Each level represents a growing threat, culminating in powerful bosses that challenge his control and force the player to adapt.

The objective is not conquest but survival—if the king falls, the kingdom falls with him. Through repeated attempts and strategic decisions, the player gradually strengthens the king’s defenses, learning from each failure. In this world, cowardice is not weakness, but a form of intelligent and calculated leadership.

## 2.2 Gameplay {#2.2-gameplay}

### **Objective**

Victory (per horde): Survive 30 turns without the king being touched by an enemy AND without 2 or more enemies simultaneously entering the 3x3 safe zone around the king.

Defeat: The king is touched by an enemy OR 2 or more enemies occupy the 3x3 safe zone at the same time.

Full game victory: Complete all 3 levels (3 hordes \+ 1 boss each) \= 12 total encounters defeated.

### **Level Structure**

| Level 1 | Skeleton King — 3 hordes (basic skeletons) \+ Skeleton King boss |
| :---- | :---- |
| **Level 2** | Ogre — 3 hordes (tougher ogres) \+ Ogre boss |
| **Level 3** | Brave King — 3 hordes (elite fast warriors) \+ Brave King boss (final) |
| **Checkpoint rule** | Death in Level 2 Horde 2 restarts from Level 2 Horde 1, NOT Level 1 |
| **On death** | Retain purchased card upgrades; lose unspent gold |
| **Level complete** | Auto-save. Session can be closed and resumed. |

### **The Game Board (8x8)**

The board is arranged in a 8-row by 8-column grid, much like a chessboard, with a total of 64 squares. The contents of the squares may be as follows:

* The King (exactly 1 at all times)

* An ally unit (Knight, Archer, Mage, etc.)

* An enemy unit

* A political card / trap (Exile, Royal Decree, etc.)

* Empty space

The king starts in the center of the board, and its 3x3 safe zone is dynamic and moves along with the king. Enemies spawn on the opposite side of the board, around row 0 or 7, with random columns, and advance one square toward the king on each of their turns. It is important to note that 3 enemies will appear on each turn.

### 

### **Turn System**

| Phase 1 — Player | Choose ONE main action: play cards (spend AP) OR move the king. Upgrading cards does NOT consume a turn. |
| :---- | :---- |
| **Phase 2 — Enemies** | All enemies move 1 tile toward the king. Ally units auto-attack if an enemy is in range. |
| **Turn limit** | Maximum 30 turns per horde. Surviving 30 turns \= automatic victory of that horde. |
| **AP accumulation** | Unspent Action Points carry over between turns with no cap. |

### **Player Actions (choose ONE per turn)**

* Play Card(s): Spend Action Points to summon units or place traps. Multiple cards can be played in one turn if enough AP is available. Cannot place on occupied tiles.

* Move the King: The king moves like a chess king — 1 tile in any of 8 directions. Cannot move to tiles occupied by allies or enemies. The safe zone moves with him.

* Upgrade Cards (special, no turn cost): Can be done at any point during the player's turn. Costs gold (20-50 per upgrade). Upgrades are PERMANENT across deaths.

### **Resource System**

| Starting AP | 5 per horde |
| :---- | :---- |
| **AP carryover** | Unused AP accumulates between turns (no limit) |
| **AP bonus** | \+5 AP upon winning a horde, applied to next horde |
| **Card cost range** | 1 to 5 AP depending on card power |
| **Gold income** | 10 gold per horde victory |
| **Gold use** | Permanent card upgrades: 20–50 gold each |
| **Gold on death** | Unspent gold is lost. Purchased upgrades are kept. |

### **Card System \- Hand Mechanics**

* At the start of each horde: receive 3 random cards from the pool of 15\.

* Upon winning a horde: receive 3 new random cards \+ keep 1 card from the previous hand (player chooses which).

* Maximum hand size: 4 cards (3 new \+ 1 carried over).

* Played cards do not return to hand until the next horde.

### 

### **Full Card Pool (15 Cards)**

| Card | Type | Cost (AP) | Stats | Effect |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| **Knight** | Attack Unit | 3 | 80 HP / 30 DMG | Melee. Moves toward nearest enemy, attacks when adjacent. |
| **Archer** | Attack Unit | 2 | 50 HP / 20 DMG | Ranged (3 tiles). Stationary. Auto-attacks nearest in range. |
| **Mage** | Attack Unit | 4 | 40 HP / 25 DMG | AoE cross pattern (3 tiles), range 2\. Fragile but powerful. |
| **Pikeman** | Attack Unit | 2 | 60 HP / 15 DMG | Fast (2 tiles/turn). Intercepts quick enemies. |
| **Wall** | Defense Unit | 3 | 150 HP / 0 DMG | Blocks tile. Enemies must destroy or go around. |
| **Squire** | Defense Unit | 2 | 70 HP / 10 DMG | Reduces 50% damage to adjacent allies. Moves 1 tile/turn. |
| **Tower** | Defense Unit | 4 | 100 HP / 35 DMG | Ranged (4 tiles). Stationary. Auto-attacks in range. |
| **Guardian** | Defense Unit | 3 | 120 HP / 25 DMG | Tanky mobile unit. Moves 1 tile/turn. Absorbs high damage. |
| **Exile** | Political | 2 | — | Trap: enemy stepping on this tile is paralyzed for 2 turns. |
| **Royal Decree** | Political | 3 | — | 3x3 push zone: enemies pushed 1 tile back each turn. |
| **Peace Treaty** | Political | 2 | — | 3x3 slow zone: enemies move at 50% speed (1 tile per 2 turns). |
| **Royal Curse** | Political | 4 | — | 3x3 debuff zone: enemies deal 50% less damage for 5 turns. |
| **Royal Guard** | Defense Unit | 2 | 90 HP / 0 DMG | Placed next to the King and follows him automatically each turn, and absorbs the damage of the first hit to the king |
| **Decoy** | Political | 1 | 30 HP / 0 DMG | Fake allies, the enemies prioritize over the king and attack it  |
| **Trench** | Defense Unit | 1 | 40 HP / 0 DMG | 1x1. The enemies next to this card can move 1 tile every 2 turns only.  |

### 

### **![][image3]**

### **Enemy Stats by Level**

| Level | Enemy | HP | Damage | Speed | Notes |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| **Level 1** | Skeleton | 50 | 15 | 1 tile/turn | Basic. Easy to intercept. |
| **Level 2** | Ogre | 80 | 25 | 1 tile/turn | Tougher. Requires stronger units. |
| **Level 3** | Elite Warrior | 100 | 35 | 2 tiles/turn | Fast. Bypasses slow defenses. |
| **Boss 1** | Skeleton King | 200 | 30 | Special | Spawns skeletons. Advances only when ally dies. |
| **Boss 2** | Ogre | 350 | 40 | Special | Spawns ogres. Same summon mechanic, harder. |
| **Boss 3** | Brave King | 500 | 50 | Special | Spawns elite warriors. Final challenge. |

### **Boss Mechanic** {#boss-mechanic}

All bosses share the same summoning cycle pattern:

* At combat start, the boss summons 1 normal enemy in an adjacent tile.

* While the summoned ally is alive, the boss does NOT move.

* The summoned ally advances toward the king normally.

* When the ally dies, the boss advances 1 tile toward the king.

* After advancing, the boss summons another ally. Cycle repeats until boss dies or reaches the king.

## 2.3 Mindset {#2.3-mindset}

In this section, we outline our five core emotions, which will guide every decision in the game design process. Every decision can be justified by a specific mechanic that brings it to life.

### **1\. Constant Tactical Tension**

Each turn will present complex challenges and force the player to make difficult decisions: 

Should you save up action points to use later when the game gets more complex and there are more powerful cards, or deploy a unit right away? 

Should you stick to your current strategy by keeping the king in position, or risk everything and move him? All of this comes at the risk of your 3x3 safety zone, as it can create constant anxiety—when two enemies approach at the same time, it can trigger a sense of paranoia or panic.

Additionally, as a game mechanic, there is a defeat condition involving the safety zone: if two enemies are inside it, with a limit of one action per turn, and these enemies advance aggressively each turn.

### **2\. Satisfaction of the Perfect Plan**

When the player places a wall, they will trigger a royal decree that pushes back three enemies in a single move, or saves up action points over several turns to deploy a tower and a mage at the same time, creating an extraordinary experience. This will allow the player to see their strategy unfold on the game board.

From a design perspective, it is essential to provide a complete view of the board; this will help players gain a comprehensive overview so they can make the best decisions, allowing political cards, area-effect cards, and point accumulation to make more sense and function as rewards earned through strategy and patience.

### **3\. Strategic Cowardice (Not Humiliating)**

The king flees and never attacks; all of this could be interpreted as cowardice or simple shame, but that is not the case. The king uses his power to defend himself, employing his political influence and his subjects to stay alive. So this can also be seen as cunning; that’s why the player acts as the mastermind behind the entire game, since they must implement different strategies to keep the king alive, making smart moves rather than weak ones.

In terms of design mechanics, the king will be depicted in pixel art. He will be portrayed with comical expressions to generate more interest in the game; for example, his faces and various expressions, such as looking scared yet maintaining a dignified appearance. Additionally, the king will be animated, with his cape visible as it moves (fluttering) while he runs. Finally, a touch of humor and irony will be added to the political cards (Exile, Royal Decree, and Peace Treaty). 

### 

### **4\. Learning Through Repetition** {#4.-learning-through-repetition}

Since this is a strategy game, it’s important to learn from your mistakes, so every death can teach you something different and important. “I should have used Exile sooner,” “Next time, it would be better to place the tower first instead of last.” That’s why the point system is essential, as it allows you to try again without having spent or lost all your progress. This helps ensure that permanent upgrades create a sense of progress, rather than the frustration of having to start all over from scratch.

Therefore, the game mechanics will feature checkpoints per level, noting that these are NOT per wave—where permanent card upgrades are earned and where waves are short, lasting a maximum of 30 turns, which is about 5 to 10 minutes.

### **5\. One More Run (Healthy Addiction)** {#5.-one-more-run-(healthy-addiction)}

One of the things that will make each attempt different is the three random cards the player receives in each wave. This prompts the player to consider how best to manage these cards. For example: “Right now I have the mage and the tower, so I can try a strategy of defending the king from a distance,” where later upgrades might tempt the player. E.g., “My knight is now going to deal \+2 damage, so I’m going to try it out.”

In terms of game mechanics, each hand is random and specific to each wave, where players have the option to keep one card across waves to develop strategies for future waves. On top of all this, an upgrade system will be implemented, showcasing the various items that can be unlocked.

## 2.4 Roguelite and Trading Card Game Elements {#2.4-roguelite-and-trading-card-game-elements}

### **Roguelite Elements**

| Roguelite Feature | Implementation in The Coward King |
| :---- | :---- |
| **Permanent progression** | Card upgrades (+damage, \+HP, \-cost) purchased with gold survive death. Each run is stronger than the last. |
| **Checkpoint system** | Death resets to the start of the current level, not the entire game. |
| **Randomized runs** | 3 random cards dealt each horde from a pool of 15\. Different builds emerge each run. |
| **Short session loop** | Each horde lasts a maximum of 30 turns. The game is designed for repeated short attempts. |
| **Meaningful failure** | Death always teaches a lesson. The game shows why you lost (king touched / safe zone breach / boss). |
| **Meta-progression** | Gold and upgrades accumulate across deaths until spent, creating a long-term power curve. |

### **Trading Card Game Elements** {#trading-card-game-elements}

| TCG Feature | Implementation in The Coward King |
| :---- | :---- |
| **Hand management** | Player holds 3-4 cards per horde, must decide when to play each one. Played cards don't return until next horde. |
| **Card pool & randomness** | 15 total cards in the pool. 3 random cards dealt per horde, creating variable strategies. |
| **Resource cost system** | Action Points (1-5 per card) mirror the mana/energy system of TCGs. AP accumulates if not spent. |
| **Card retention choice** | Between hordes, the player keeps 1 card from their previous hand — a deck-building decision. |
| **Card upgrade / crafting** | Permanent upgrades (+damage, \+HP, \-cost) mirror card enhancement in TCGs and CCGs. |
| **Synergy potential** | Combining cards (e.g., Wall \+ Tower, Exile \+ Mage) creates powerful combos that reward strategic thinking. |

## 2.5 Visual Style {#2.5-visual-style}

### **Art Direction**

Coward King will feature a pixel art aesthetic, using 16x32-pixel sprites to create units and keep the board clean. The visual style we aim for is a comical medieval look, where the king appears exaggeratedly frightened (with wide-open eyes and his cape billowing in the wind) and the enemies have a cartoonish, not entirely threatening style.

| Art style | Pixel art, 16x16 and 32x32 sprites |
| :---- | :---- |
| **Board style** | Checkerboard with alternating neutral tones (light gray / cream). Safe zone highlighted in soft green. |
| **Color palette** | Muted medieval palette: stone grays, forest greens, parchment yellows, deep reds for enemies. |
| **Animation** | 2-4 frames per unit (idle \+ attack/move). King has: idle, run (fleeing), celebrate, panic. |
| **UI style** | Card game UI — cards displayed as rectangles with icon, name, cost, and description. Clean sans-serif font. |
| **Tone** | Comedic but readable. Humor through the king's expressions, not through chaotic visuals. |
| **References** | Slay the Spire (card UI), Into the Breach (board clarity), Dicey Dungeons (character expression). |

### **Visual Justification** {#visual-justification}

Using pixel art for this video game is essential, and this can be explained by the following three reasons:

* The team consists of three members, none of whom are experienced artists, so by using pixel art and 16x32 sprites, we can work with tools like Asperite. On the other hand, since we have limited resources, we can use free temporary resources like Kenney.nl, which allows us to continue development even before all the graphic assets are finished.


* In terms of readability, using pixel art greatly helps maintain clarity on the grid/board where the game is played. This is because it makes it easier to distinguish characters or objects by their silhouette alone. This would also enhance gameplay and tactical agility by making things easier to see; analysis could be done more quickly.

* Finally, there is the harmony of tones: using pixel art supports the medieval mechanical aesthetic the video game aims to achieve. The king’s exaggerated expressions work better here than they would with realistic or vector-based scales.

On the other hand, we also aim for roguelite elements and replayability through these decisions, where there are changing configurations and situations within a fixed structure. All of this aligns with how our game’s design is described.

# **3\. Technical** {#3.-technical}

## 3.1 Screens {#3.1-screens}

**Home Page (Menu)**

 It is the first thing you see opening the game. Contains the options to start a new game, resume a game, and view your stats. Also will be included the options page where you can control the volume and display settings.

The menu includes:

1. **Login / Sign Up**  
   * Allows the player to create an account or log into an existing one.  
   * Stores player progress, statistics, upgrades, and saved checkpoints.  
   * Required before accessing saved progress.  
2. **Start New Game**  
   * Begins a new run from Level 1\.  
   * Resets current run progress but keeps account-based permanent data if applicable.  
3. **Resume Game**  
   * Loads the player’s last saved checkpoint.  
   * Available only if an auto-save exists after completing a full level.  
4. **Stats**  
   * Displays player statistics such as:  
     * Total runs attempted  
     * Levels completed  
     * Enemies defeated  
     * Bosses defeated  
     * Cards upgraded  
     * Total gold earned  
5. **Options**  
   * Allows the player to adjust:  
     * Master volume  
     * Music volume  
     * Sound effects volume  
     * Display settings  
     * Fullscreen/windowed mode  
6. **Credits**  
   * Shows the development team and project information.

**![][image9]**

**Game Screen (Board)**

 The primary gameplay screen. Divided into functional displays:

* **Board Zone**: The **8x8** board placed in the center of the screen.Where the King will be displayed with allies, enemies, traps and the safe zone highlighted in a 3x3 area around the king.  
* **Hand Zone**:In the bottom of the screen, it will show the hand of cards the player disposes of to defend the kings, up to 4 cards containing its name, AP, cost, icon and description.  
* **HUD**: Shown in the top of the screen, demonstrating current turn, out of 30, available AP, accumulated gold, current level and horde.  
* **Pause Menu**: Accessible during battle. Contains options to resume, adjust settings, or return to the menu.

![][image10]

**Horde TransitionScreen (Card Retention)**

Appears after winning a horde, this allows the player to choose which 1 card from their previous hand to keep before receiving 3 new random cards.

**Upgrade / Shop Screen**

 Accessible to open between hordes and levels. All 15 cards are displayed with the current level of the card and cost to upgrade. Allowing to improve HP, damage, and AP cost.

**Game Over Screen**

 Triggered when the King is touched by an enemy or 2 or more enemies simultaneously occupy the 3×3 safe zone. Displays the level and horde reached, gold lost, and upgrades retained. Offers options to retry from the current level's Horde 1 or return to the main menu.

**Victory Screen**

 Triggered upon completing all 3 levels, 12 total encounters.

## 3.2 Controls {#3.2-controls}

The game is controlled entirely with the mouse. No keyboard input is required during gameplay.

| Action | Input |
| :---: | :---: |
| Select a card from hand | Left click on card |
| Place a unit or trap on the board | Left click on target tile |
| Move the King | Left click on a valid adjacent tile |
| Cancel selection | Left click on empty area / right click |
| Open Upgrade menu | Left click on upgrade button (HUD) |
| Confirm upgrade | Left click on upgrade option |
| End turn / confirm action | Left click on "End Turn" button |
| Open pause menu | Left click on pause button |
| Navigate menus | Left click |

Cards and tiles provide visual hover feedback (highlight) to guide player interaction. Invalid placements (occupied tiles, out-of-range) are indicated visually before the click is confirmed.

## 3.3 Mechanics {#3.3-mechanics}

**Turn Phase System**

Each turn is divided in two phases:

1.  Player Phase: the player has one main action available, play one or more cards with AP cost or move the king one tile to whatever direction. Also can upgrade his cards at any moment during this phase without consuming the turn. If played the card and deployed, the player can also choose where to attack with this troop.  
2. Enemy Phase: During this phase the enemies advance one tile threatening the king or allies unities.

**AP System (Action Points)**

* In each horde the player starts with 5 AP.  
* Unspent AP carries over between turns, allowing players to save for high cost plays or strategic ends.  
* A bonus of \+5 AP as a reward for winning a horde is applied to the next horde's starting pool.  
* Cards cost 1–5 AP depending on their power level.

**Card Selection & Placement**

* The player clicks a card in the hand zone to select it.  
* Political cards (Exile, Royal Decree, Peace Treaty, Royal Curse) activate a zone effect on placement.  
* Cards cannot be placed on occupied tiles.

**King Movement**

* Clicking the King highlights the available tiles for movement (like chess king rules).  
* Clicking a highlighted tile moves the King and shifts the 3×3 safe zone with him.  
* The King cannot move to tiles occupied by allies or enemies.

**Hand Randomization**

* At the start of each horde, the player receives 3 randomly drawn cards from the pool of 15\.  
* After winning a horde, the player selects 1 card from their previous hand to retain, then draws 3 new random cards, for a maximum hand size of 4\.

**Enemy Spawn System**

* At the start of each enemy phase, 3 new enemies spawn on the opposite end of the board at random columns.  
* Each enemy advances 1 tile per turn toward the King (Elite Warriors advance 2 tiles per turn).  
* Boss enemies follow a separate spawning function. They spawn one normal enemy, remain stationary while it lives, advance 1 tile when it dies and then repeat.

**Card Upgrade System**

* Accessible via the upgrade menu during the player's turn with no turn cost or even between hordes via the shop screen.  
* Each upgrade costs from 20 to 50 gold and permanently improves a card's stats.  
* Upgrades persist across deaths.  
* If gold is not spent, then is lost on death, purchased upgrades are always retained.

**Save & Checkpoint System**

* The game auto saves upon completing a full level (3 hordes \+ boss).  
* On death, the player returns to Horde 1 of the level where they died.  
* Sessions can be closed and resumed from the last completed level checkpoint.

# **4\. Level Design** {#4.-level-design}

## 4.1 Themes {#4.1-themes}

The game is divided in three different levels, each one with a different theme that changes throughout the game, while the board keeps the same across levels, only the background changes based on the final Boss of the level. If the boss is a Skeleton, then the background will be inspired by bones and skeletons. 

### Level 1 Skeleton King, Catacombs {#level-1-skeleton-king,-catacombs}

**Ambience** The atmosphere is dim and unsettling. Cold stone walls, flickering torches, and crumbling archways frame the board. Color palette: stone grays, cold blues, faded yellows from torchlight.

**Objects**

Ambient*:*

* Crumbling stone walls and gothic arches in the background  
* Flickering torch sconces on the sides  
* Cobwebs and scattered bones as decorative elements  
* Faint mist at the bottom of the screen

Interactive*:*

* **Skeletons** (50 HP / 15 DMG / 1 tile per turn). Basic enemies that spawn 3 per turn on row 0 and advance toward the King.  
* **Skeleton King** (Boss 200 HP / 30 DMG). Remains stationary while its summoned skeleton ally is alive, and advances 1 tile upon its death, then summons another enemy.

**Challenges**

* Introduces the core loop: AP management, card placement, and safe zone defense.  
* Enemy stats are low, giving the player room to experiment with different card combinations.  
* The boss mechanic is introduced for the first time, where players must learn to kill summoned allies to force the boss to move and become vulnerable to pass to the next level.

![][image11]

##### Level 2 Ogre, Dungeon {#level-2-ogre,-dungeon}

**Ambience** The environment shifts to a darker  more oppressive dungeon with hints of a gnarled forest beyond the walls. Heavier shadows, mossy stone, and deep reds replace the cold grays of Level 1\. Trying to simulate more danger. Color palette: deep greens, dark browns, muted reds, murky shadows.

**Objects**

Ambient:

* Mossy dungeon walls with iron-barred windows  
* Gnarled tree roots breaking through the stone floor  
* Hanging chains and dim lanterns  
* Puddles of murky water reflecting enemy silhouettes

Interactive:

* **Ogres** (80 HP / 25 DMG / 1 tile per turn) — tougher enemies that require stronger defensive units or multi-card combos to handle efficiently  
* **Ogre Boss** (350 HP / 40 DMG) — same summoning cycle as Level 1's boss but with significantly higher stats; summoned ogres also take more effort to eliminate

**Challenges**

* Higher enemy HP demands better AP management — cheap cards alone are insufficient  
* Players must rely more on unit synergies (e.g., Wall \+ Tower, Guardian \+ Archer) to survive all 3 hordes  
* The boss fight requires sustained damage output across multiple summon cycles

![][image12]

##### Level 3 Brave King, Castle {#level-3-brave-king,-castle}

**Ambience** The final level takes place in the throne room, the heart of the enemy kingdom. The atmosphere is legendary, rich ornaments, tall windows, and golden candlelight which create a visually striking background. The color palette combines deep reds, gold accents, royal purples, and dramatic lighting.

**Objects**

Ambient:

* Grand stone throne visible in the background  
* Tall windows  
* Royal banners and battle worn flags  
* Fallen armor and broken shields as environmental detail  
* Gold everywhere 

**Interactive:**

* Elite Warriors (100 HP / 35 DMG / 2 tiles per turn), the most dangerous regular enemy. Their doubled movement bypasses the slow movement traps and demands clever board responses.  
* Brave King (Boss 500 HP / 50 DMG), final challenge. Same summoning cycle but with elite warriors as allies of the boss, meaning each ally advances twice per turn and is harder to intercept.

**Challenges:**

* Elite Warriors 2 tile movement breaks many defensive formations that worked in earlier levels, forcing the player to adapt their strategy  
* Political cards (Exile, Peace Treaty) become critical for slowing or immobilizing fast enemies  
* The final boss's summoned allies are themselves a severe threat, requiring the player to balance killing the ally quickly while protecting the safe zone

![][image13]

## 

## 

## 4.2 Game Flow {#4.2-game-flow}

The game progresses linearly from the main menu through three levels, each composed of 3 hordes and 1 boss fight, for a total of 12 encounters.

Main Menu  
Level 1 \- Horde 1 (win: card retention screen, next horde)  
Level 1 \- Horde 2  
Level 1 \- Horde 3  
Level 1 \- Boss (Skeleton King) (win: auto-save, Level 2\)

Level 2 \- Horde 1  
Level 2 \- Horde 2  
Level 2 \- Horde 3  
Level 2 \- Boss (Ogre Boss) (win: auto-save, Level 3\)

Level 3 \- Horde 1  
Level 3 \- Horde 2  
Level 3 \- Horde 3  
Level 3 \- Boss (Brave King):  Final Encounter (win)

Victory Screen

**Transition rules:**

Between every horde the player sees the card retention screen, where they choose 1 card from their current hand to carry into the next horde before drawing 3 new random cards. The upgrade shop is always available, the game also auto saves at the current level.

After a death  the player is returned to Horde 1 of the level where they died. Purchased upgrades are always retained, but unspent gold is lost. The player cannot select a starting level, progression is always sequential so that the difficulty curve is experienced.

# **5\. Development** {#5.-development}

## 5.1 Abstract Classes (Components) {#5.1-abstract-classes-(components)}

This section will define the core architecture of our video game, where abstract classes will be used to represent the fundamental components—which are shared by the various objects in the game. Therefore, these classes are not only instantiated directly but also have a complete structure and reusable logic.

### **GameObject (Base Class)** {#gameobject-(base-class)}

Represents any entity that exists in the game (King, enemies, allies, tiles, etc.).

Attributes:

* position → Grid position on the x and y axes.  
* type → This is the identifier (King, enemy, ally, trap).  
* isActive → Boolean state to indicate whether it is active or not.

Methods:

* update() → updates the object's state each turn, to check the elements present in each turn  
* render() → draws the object on screen, to draw the current objects and any new ones that may have been added  
* interact() → defines interaction behavior

### 

### **Unit (Abstract Class)** {#unit-(abstract-class)}

Extends GameObject. Represents any moving or combat-capable entity.

Attributes:

* hp → health points \- To view the health of units in combat, whether they are “good” or “bad”  
* damage → attack value \- The damage dealt by characters on both sides  
* speed → tiles per turn

Methods:

* move() → handles movement logic \- To control how the unit moves. The default movement is 1 tile.  
* attack() → executes attack if in range \- Generates the attack movement  
* PoliticAttack() → executes attack when the political card is played and analyzes the effect that will be triggered when used  
* takeDamage(amount) → reduces HP \- A way to update character damage on the battlefield.

### **Card (Abstract Class)** {#card-(abstract-class)}

Represents a playable card from the player’s hand.

Attributes:

* cost → AP cost \- The cost of the cards to be able to use them  
* name → card name   
* type → attack / defense / political \- Select which of the three card types it is.

Methods:

* activate(targetTile) → ejecuta el efecto en el tablero  
* getValidTiles() → devuelve las posiciones de colocación válidas

### **Board (Component)** {#board-(component)}

Handles the 8×8 grid system.

Attributes:

* grid\[8\]\[8\] → stores all objects \- generate the board/battlefield  
* safeZone → dynamic 3×3 area around the King \- generate the King's safe zone

Methods:

* placeObject(obj, tile) → to place objects so they are within the board  
* removeObject(tile) → to remove tiles  
* updateSafeZone() → to move the king's safe zone to another part of the map

### **TurnManager (Component)** {#turnmanager-(component)}

Controls game flow.

Attributes:

* currentPhase → Player / Enemy. To determine whose turn it is.  
* turnCount → Keep track of the number of turns so we can monitor whose turn it is. We’ll also use this condition later so that the player wins after a certain number of turns.  
* maxTurns → Keep track of the number of turns so we can control whose turn it is. We’ll also use this condition later so that the player wins after a certain number of turns.

Methods:

* nextPhase()  
* startTurn()  
* endTurn()

## 

## 5.2 Derived Classes (Component Compositions) {#5.2-derived-classes-(component-compositions)}

These classes extend abstract classes and implement specific behaviors for the game.

### **King (extends Unit)** {#king-(extends-unit)}

Special unit controlled by the player.

**Behavior:**

* Cannot attack  
* Moves 1 tile in any direction (chess king movement)  
* Updates safe zone position

### **Enemy Classes (extends Unit)** {#enemy-classes-(extends-unit)}

#### **Skeleton** {#skeleton}

* Low HP and damage  
* Moves 1 tile per turn

#### **Ogre** {#ogre}

* Higher HP and damage  
* Requires stronger units to defeat

#### **Elite Warrior** {#elite-warrior}

* Moves 2 tiles per turn  
* High threat to safe zone

### **Boss Classes (extends Unit)** {#boss-classes-(extends-unit)}

#### **Skeleton King / Ogre / Brave King** {#skeleton-king-/-ogre-/-brave-king}

**Shared Behavior:**

* Summons 1 enemy  
* Does not move until summoned enemy dies  
* Advances 1 tile after summon dies

### **Ally Units (extends Unit)** {#ally-units-(extends-unit)}

#### **Examples:** {#examples:}

* **Knight** → melee attacker  
* **Archer** → ranged unit  
* **Mage** → AoE damage  
* **Guardian** → tank

**Behavior:**

* Auto-move or stay depending on type  
* Auto-attack enemies in range

### **Trap / Political Cards (extends GameObject)** {#trap-/-political-cards-(extends-gameobject)}

#### **Examples:** {#examples:-1}

* **Exile** → stuns enemy  
* **Royal Decree** → pushes enemies  
* **Peace Treaty** → slows enemies  
* **Royal Curse** → reduces damage

**Behavior:**

* Activate when enemy enters tile or zone  
* Affect multiple tiles (AoE mechanics)

### 

### 

### 

### **Hand System (Component)** {#hand-system-(component)}

Manages player cards.

**Attributes:**

* cards\[\] → current hand (max 4\)

**Methods:**

* drawCards()  
* playCard(card, tile)  
* retainCard(card)

### **EnemySpawner (Component)** {#enemyspawner-(component)}

Controls enemy generation.

**Behavior:**

* Spawns 3 enemies per turn  
* Random column placement  
* Fixed spawn row (top or bottom)

### **UpgradeSystem (Component)** {#upgradesystem-(component)}

Handles meta-progression.

**Attributes:**

* gold  
* upgrades\[\]

**Methods:**

* upgradeCard(card)  
* applyUpgradeEffects()

# **Schedule** {#schedule}

The development of The Coward King will be organized into **progressive development phases over a 8-week period**, instead of fixed weekly tasks. This allows flexibility in the workflow while ensuring all core systems are implemented efficiently.

Each phase focuses on a specific aspect of the game, prioritizing core mechanics first, followed by systems, interface, and final polish. Continuous testing and iteration will be performed throughout all phases. It’s worth noting that this is because our team consists of people who don’t have much experience programming video games, so this schedule will be organized according to the game’s priorities.

## Development Phases {#development-phases}

### **1\. Core Systems Development** {#1.-core-systems-development}

* Define base architecture of the game  
* Implement core classes:  
  * GameObject  
  * Unit  
  * Card  
* Create board system (8x8 grid)  
* Basic rendering setup (canvas \+ visual grid)

### **2\. Gameplay Mechanics Implementation** {#2.-gameplay-mechanics-implementation}

* Implement turn system:  
  * Player Phase / Enemy Phase  
* Implement Action Points (AP system)  
* Implement King movement  
* Define interaction rules (movement, placement, restrictions)

### **3\. Card System Development** {#3.-card-system-development}

* Implement:  
  * Card selection (click-based)  
  * Card placement logic  
* Define valid tiles for placement  
* Implement initial card behaviors (units and traps)

### **4\. Enemy System Implementation** {#4.-enemy-system-implementation}

* Develop enemy movement toward the King  
* Implement spawn system (3 enemies per turn)  
* Define enemy types and behaviors  
* Implement collision and interaction with allies

### **5\. Combat & Interaction Systems** {#5.-combat-&-interaction-systems}

* Implement auto-attack mechanics  
* Damage and health system  
* Area effects (AoE, zones, traps)  
* Safe zone logic (3×3 around the King)

### **6\. Boss & Progression Systems** {#6.-boss-&-progression-systems}

* Implement boss mechanics (summoning cycle)  
* Define win/lose conditions  
* Implement level progression system  
* Ensure checkpoint behavior per level

### **7\. Roguelite Systems** {#7.-roguelite-systems}

* Implement card randomization per horde  
* Implement card retention system  
* Develop upgrade system:  
  * Gold accumulation  
  * Permanent upgrades

### **8\. User Interface & Screens** {#8.-user-interface-&-screens}

* Develop:  
  * Main Menu  
  * Game Screen (board \+ hand \+ HUD)  
  * Game Over Screen  
  * Victory Screen  
* Implement HUD elements:  
  * AP  
  * Turn counter  
  * Gold

### **9\. Visual & Audio Implementation** {#9.-visual-&-audio-implementation}

* Integrate sprites (units, enemies, board, cards)  
* Add visual feedback (hover, highlights)  
* Implement sound effects:  
  * Click interactions  
  * Card placement  
  * Enemy actions

### **10\. Testing & Final Polish** {#10.-testing-&-final-polish}

* Debugging and optimization  
* Gameplay balancing:  
  * Enemy difficulty  
  * Card effectiveness  
* Improve user experience  
* Final adjustments and preparation for delivery
